title: Listening
hookLine: a reply loading while someone talks; three monks who set their own plans aside
tomorrow: a king comes to confess something terrible. what does the Buddha say?

cards: Watch two people talk and it's often visible: one is speaking, and the other has a reply loading, mouth half open, waiting for a gap.
It happens at dinner tables, in group calls, in the car on the way home, and the speaker can usually feel it. What changes when the reply stops loading? The other person can finally finish.
And a story that's been waiting years to be told sometimes comes out all at once, over breakfast.

teach.b: In one sutta, the Buddha visits three monks living together in a forest park: Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila. How do you get along so well? he asks.
Anuruddha answers: I think, why don't I set aside what I want to do, and do what these friends want? We're different in body, but one in mind.

The suttas picture them as milk and water, blending, looking at each other with kind eyes. Notice what Anuruddha does not say. He doesn't say they agree on everything, or that nobody ever wants something different.
He says each one sets his own plan aside, for a while, to take in the others. That, for a moment, is what listening is.
The modern teacher Thich Nhat Hanh called it deep listening: hearing someone with one aim, to help them suffer a little less, and no reply ready.

teach.h: A WEEK FROM MONEY TO WORDS.
teach.b: Listening, then, sits at the end of a week that ran from money to words. Four parts: live on one, put two to work, keep one back. A part given, woven into the part you live on.
Free of debt, its own quiet happiness. Enough, light as a bird with only its wings.
Kind at home, where it's tested. The right time, after true and helpful. Six ways of handling what we have and what we say.
And now the other half of speech, the half that makes the rest land: the ear.

how: Some Buddhist communities practice listening as part of right speech; in some, a talking-stick or bell circle lets each person speak while the others listen without replying.

o: setting your own reply aside to take someone in
hearing the Buddha's voice inside your own mind
staying silent until it's your turn to speak

games.q: the week, from money to words — tap the pairs.
p: live on one, two to work, one kept back
owing no one, its own happiness
set aside what I want to do

s: listening, in this sutta, is just staying quiet while you plan your answer
Anuruddha sets his own plan aside and does what his friends want: one in mind.
the three monks are pictured as milk and water, blending
different in body, one in mind, looking at each other with kind eyes.
the Sigalovada tells householders to give away the fourth part
the fourth part is kept for hard times; giving runs through the part you live on.

games.q: your grandpa starts telling a story you've heard many times. you could finish it for him, or check your phone. what does Anuruddha's way point to?
o: finish it for him kindly, so he knows you remember.
check your phone; he won't mind, he's told it before.
set your own plan aside and take the story in, as if new.
games.why: Anuruddha sets aside what he wants and does what his friends want. listening is that, for a few minutes: one mind, no reply loading.

practice: Listen to the room as if it were someone talking to you: the hum, a car outside, a voice through the wall.

Don't name the sounds or answer them; just receive each one until it's finished, the way you'd let a friend finish a sentence. When a thought starts loading, set it down, the way Anuruddha set down his plans.

wordCard.voice: Listening: setting your own reply aside long enough to take someone in, all the way to the end. Different in body, one in mind, like milk and water.

carryVoice: One word to carry: listen, before the reply loads. Three of four, and the week is closed.
